items.t: Anglo-American Exchange in Postwar Sculpture

This case study looks at the management of Port Arthur Historic Site in Australia by the Port Arthur Historic Site Management Authority (PAHSMA) since 1987. PAHSMA is a government business enterprise created by the Tasmanian State government. Conservation and stewardship of Port Arthur as a heritage site is the primary objective of PAHSMA in managing the site.

items.t: The Stammheim Missal

The Stammheim Missal is one of the most visually dazzling and theologically ambitious works of German Romanesque art. Containing the text recited by the priest and the chants sung by the choir at mass, the manuscript was produced in Lower Saxony around 1160 at Saint Michael's Abbey at Hildesheim, a celebrated abbey in medieval Germany.

items.d: Conservation is a core value for most archaeological societies. It is highlighted in their codes of ethics, statements of mission, and governance. In recognition of this, the World Archaeological Congress, with the Getty Conservation Institute and a consortium of other conservation organizations, brought together scholars working throughout the globe to discuss vital issues that affect archaeological heritage today.

items.t: Antiquity & Photography: Early Views of Ancient Mediterranean Sites
items.a: Claire L. Lyons, John K. Papadopoulos, Lindsey S. Stewart, and Andrew Szegedy-Maszak
items.d:
Following the invention of the daguerreotype and calotype processes in 1839, views of ruins, classical statuary, and the antiquities of the Mediterranean and the Orient were among the first images produced by pioneer photographers. The unique accuracy and immediacy of photographs fundamentally changed aesthetic and scholarly approaches to the artifacts of the past.
This pathbreaking book, which coincided with the in

items.t: The Silver Canvas: Daguerreotype Masterpieces from the J. Paul Getty Museum
items.a: Bates Lowry and Isabel Barrett Lowry
items.d:
In 1835, Louis Daguerre–French inventor, painter, and stage designer—devised one of the first practical photographic processes, the "daguerreotype."
In the Getty Museum's photographs collection are nearly two thousand daguerreotypes, including such notable examples as John Plumbe's The United States Capitol, one of the earliest known photographs of the building; an 1849 image of Edgar Allan Poe; and the documentatio

items.t: Courbet and the Modern Landscape
items.a: Mary Morton and Charlotte Eyerman, with an essay by Dominique de Font-Réaulx
items.d: While the large-scale figural works of Gustave Courbet’s early to mid-career—pictures such as Burial at Ornans, The Stonebreakers, and The Studio of the Painter—are of signal importance to the history of Western art, it is in the genre of landscape that the artist laid the groundwork for a vital current of Modernist painting. items.t: Pontormo: Portrait of a Halberdier
items.d:
Much has been written about the identity of the sitter in this portrait by Pontormo. In 1568 the most famous contemporary recorder of artists' lives, the painter Giorgio Vasari, noted that Pontormo had painted a beautiful work, a portrait of Francesco Guardi depicted as a soldier during the 1528 siege of Florence. However, in 1612 the name of Cosimo I de' Medici was attached to a description of the portrait.

items.t: The Conservation of Archaeological Sites in the Mediterranean Region: An International Conference Organized by the Getty Conservation Institute and the J. Paul Getty Museum, 6–12 May 1995
items.a: Edited by Marta de la Torre
items.d:
One of the greatest challenges faced today by those responsible for ancient cultural sites is that of maintaining the delicate balance between conserving these fragile resources and making them available to increasing numbers of visitors. Tourism, unchecked development, and changing environmental conditions threaten significant historical sites throughout the world.

items.t: Joséphine and the Arts of the Empire
items.a: Edited by Eleanor P. DeLorme; with contributions by Bernard Chevallier, Kimberly Chrisman-Campbell, David Gilbert, Christopher Hartop, Peter Mitchell, Tamara Pr
items.d: Renowned for her exquisite taste, her talent for attracting the most gifted artists and artisans of her time, and her ability to further their careers, Empress Joséphine, wife of Napoleon Bonaparte, had a profound and lasting effect on the arts of all Europe. Joséphine and the Arts of the Empire presents, for the first time in a single volume, evidence of Joséphine's far-reaching impact on painting, sculpture, garden

items.t: Luxury Arts of the Renaissance
items.d: Today we associate Renaissance arts with painting, sculpture, and architecture. Yet gem-studded goldwork and richly embellished armor; splendid tapestries, embroideries, and textiles; ephemeral multimedia spectacles; and other opulent creations were consistently more celebrated by contemporaries. items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: Preserving the Legacy of 20th-Century Art
items.a: With contributions from Neville Agnew, Tracy Bartley, Mildred Constantine, Vladimir Kucera, Bo Rendahl, Ed Ruscha, David A. Scott, and Ann Temkin
items.d: This issue contains a feature about preserving art of the 20th century; a conversation with artist Ed Ruscha about experimental art materials and the artist’s role in preservation; and articles on the recent Conservation Institute conference "Mortality Immortality? The Legacy of 20th-Century Art," and rock art.

items.t: Making Architecture: The Getty Center
items.a: Richard Meier, Ada Louise Huxtable, Stephen D. Rountree, and  Harold M. Williams
items.d:
This volume completes the documentation of the planning, design, and construction of the Getty Center begun in The Getty Center (1991). Designed by Richard Meier and Partners, the Getty Center sits atop a stunning 110-acre hilltop in west Los Angeles and is the new home for the Museum, the five Institutes, and the Grant Program that make up the J. Paul Getty Trust.

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: The Restoration of an Industrial Community
items.a: With contributions from Neville Agnew, Mildred Constantine, Jeffrey Levin, Barry Munitz, Francesca Piqué, and Giora Solar
items.d: This issue contains a feature about urban conservation, with a focus on the revitalization of an industrial district of Culver City, in Los Angeles; a conversation with Barry Munitz, President and Chief Executive Officer of the Getty Trust; and articles on preservation in Los Angeles, and the conservation of The Last Judgment Mosaic in the St. Vitus Cathedral in Prague Castle.

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: Illicit Trade in Cultural Objects
items.a: With contributions from Marta de la Torre, Sarah Jackson, Maria Papageorge Kouroupas, Engin Özgen, and Jane Siena Talley
items.d: This issue contains a feature about illicit trade in cultural objects; a conversation with Engin Özgen, former director general of monuments and museums in Turkey; and articles on fighting art theft, and a recent partnership between the Conservation Institute and the government of the Netherlands to initiate conservation programs in St. Petersburg, Rusia.

items.t: Giambattista Tiepolo: Fifteen Oil Sketches
items.d:
Giambattista Tiepolo (1696–1770) was the greatest Italian painter of the eighteenth century, best known for his monumental frescoes and epic altarpieces. The scale of these paintings is immense, even overpowering. Yet some of Tiepolo's finest work can be found in the small oil sketches that he often made in preparation for these grand commissions.
Published to coincide with an exhibition at the Getty Museum from May

items.t: French Tapestries and Textiles in the J. Paul Getty Museum
items.d: French Tapestries and Textiles is a survey of the Getty Museum’s seventeenth- and eighteenth-century French textiles—one of the world’s finest collections. Featuring twenty-five extraordinary tapestries woven at the Gobelins and Beauvais manufactories, the catalogue also highlights three carpets, two knotted-pile screens, and two sets of embroidered bed hangings, one of which is the only complete lit à la duchesse su

items.t: Conservation of the Last Judgment Mosaic, St. Vitus Cathedral, Prague
items.a: Edited by Francesca Pique and Dusan C. Stulik
items.d: Illustrated in color throughout, this handsome volume presents selected papers from an international symposium held in June 2001 marking the completion of a ten-year project to conserve the Last Judgment mosaic, at St. Vitus Cathedral in Prague. The project was a partnership between the Office of the President of the Czech Republic, the Prague Castle Administration, and the Getty Conservation Institute. The goal of t

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: The Getty Conservation Institute: Present and Future
items.a: With contributions from Miguel Angel Corzo, Leilani Lattin Duke, Eleanor Fink, Al Gore, Deborah Marrow, Salvatore Settis, Jane Siena Talley, and John Walsh
items.d: This issue contains a feature about the Getty Conservation Institute’s move to the Getty Center; a conversation with Vice President Al Gore; and articles on conservation and programs of the Getty Trust, and new projects of the Conservation Institute.

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: Preservation of Archaeological Sites
items.a: With contributions from Neville Agnew, Mario Bravo, Marta de la Torre, Martha Demas, Abilio Dias Fernandes, Margaret G. H. MacLean, and Colin Pearson
items.d: This issue contains a feature about the preservation of archaeological sites; a conversation with Abilio Dias Fernandes, mayor of Evora, Portugal; and articles on archaeological heritage in the Mediterranean Region, and preserving collections in tropical countries.

items.t: Cézanne in the Studio: Still Life in Watercolors
items.d:
In the last years of his life Paul Cézanne produced a stunning series of watercolors, many of them still lifes. Still Life with Blue Pot is one of these late masterpieces that is now in the collection of the Getty Museum.
In Cézanne in the Studio: Still Life in Watercolors, Carol Armstrong places this great painting within the context of Cézanne’s artistic and psychological development and of the history of the genr

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: Conserving Historic Centers
items.a: With contributions from Mahasti Afshar, Lori Anglin, David de Souza, Jeffrey Levin, Roberto Nardi, Anil Rao, and Catherine Sease
items.d: This issue contains a feature about conserving historic centers; a conversation with Anil Rao and David de Souza about the Picture Mumbai project; and articles on the GCI’s Landmarks Campaign, and the conservation of mosaics in situ.

items.t: Roger Fenton: Pasha and Bayadère
items.d:
Roger Fenton's photograph Pasha and Bayadere is a fascinating image in its own right and is an expression of a more general Orientalist craze that grew steadily stronger during the nineteenth century in Europe.

items.a: Réalisé par Valerie Dorge et Sharon L. Jones
items.d: Building an Emergency Plan provides a step-by-step guide that a cultural institution can follow to develop its own emergency preparedness and response strategy. This workbook is divided into three parts that address the three groups generally responsible for developing and implementing emergency procedures—institution directors, emergency preparedness managers, and departmental team leaders—and discuss the role each

items.t: Gardens of the Roman World
items.d: Romans loved their gardens, whether they were the grand gardens of imperial country estates or the small private spaces tucked behind city houses. Gardens were treasured both as places for relaxation and as plots to grow ornamental plants, fruits, and vegetables. The soothing sound of fountains often added further to the pleasures of life in the garden. Romans constructed gardens in every corner of their empire, from

items.t: Creación de un plan de emergencia: Guía para museos y otras instituciones culturales
items.a: Recopilada por Valerie Dorge y Sharon L. Jones
items.d:
When an emergency strikes, is your cultural institution prepared to protect the people on-site, the premises, and its collections from harm? Building an Emergency Plan offers step-by-step guidance to help cultural institutions develop their own emergency preparedness and response strategies. 
This workbook is divided into three parts to individually address the groups generally responsible for delveloping and implem

items.t: Conservation and Seismic Strengthening of Byzantine Churches in Macedonia
items.a: Predrag Gavrilović, William S. Ginnell, Veronika Sendova, and Lazar Šumanov
items.d:
Between the ninth and fourteenth century, hundreds of architecturally exquisite Byzantine churches were built in the area now known as the Republic of Macedonia. The condition of these buildings has been of ongoing concern because of deterioration and destruction from forces both human and natural, including devastating earthquakes.
This book summarizes the results of a four-year study to develop and test seismic re

items.t: Jan Steen: The Drawing Lesson
items.d: “Clear, solid, palpable”—this is the world of the Dutch painters of the seventeenth century, a world in which the surfaces and scenes of every day life are rendered with impeccable care and illuminated by clear, soft light. items.t: The Appian Way: From Its Foundation to the Middle Ages
items.a: Edited by Ivana della Portella, photography by Franco Mammana
items.d: The Appian Way was the first great artery from Rome to southern Italy and the model for all roads originating in the ancient capital. Conceived by Appius Claudius in 312 BC, the thoroughfare provided easy access to Capua, the most important junction in southern Italy, and facilitated Roman expansion into the southern peninsula. items.t: Anthony van Dyck: Thomas Howard, The Earl of Arundel
items.d:
Anthony van Dyck’s portrait of Thomas Howard was made during the artist’s first visit to London and marked the beginning of Van Dyck’s brilliant international career. Thomas Howard, a prominent member of the court of King James I, was to become one of the most enlightened collectors and patrons England has ever known.
In this probing study, Christopher White provides a history both of Thomas Howard and Van Dyck, the

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: The St. Petersburg International Center for Preservation
items.a: With contributions from Neville Agnew, Zhores Alferov, Wilbur Faulk, Jeffrey Levin, and Jane Slate Siena
items.d: This issue contains a feature about the St. Petersburg International Center for Preservation; a conversation with Zhores Alferov, the vice president of the Russian Academy of Sciences; and articles on preserving Russia’s collections in changing times, and adapting technology for conservation.

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: The Great Murals
items.a: With contributions from Miguel Angel Corzo, Peter Dorman, Margaret G. H. MacLean, Nicholas Stanley-Price, and Sandy Silver
items.d: This issue contains a feature about conserving the rock art of Baja California; a conversation with Peter Dorman, field director of the Epigraphic Survey of the University of Chicago’s Oriental Institute; and articles on documentation and conservation, and the GCI in transition.

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: History Told on Walls
items.a: With contributions from Selma Al-Radi, Rachida de Souza, William S. Ginell, Francesca Piqué, and Leslie Rainer
items.d: This issue contains a feature about the Bas-Reliefs of the Royal Palaces of Abomey; a conversation with Rachida de Souza, director of the Republic of Benin’s Department of Cultural Heritage; and articles on the Getty Seismic Adobe Project and cultural heritage in Lebanon.

items.t: Had Gadya: The Only Kid; Facsimile of El Lissitsky’s Edition of 1919
items.d: This illustrated version of the popular Passover song “Had Gadya” was the wonderfully playful offspring of the avant-garde artist El Lissitzky (1890–1941). It dates to a little-known period early in his career when he immersed himself in the Jewish cultural renaissance that flourished in Russia from roughly 1912 to the early 1920s. items.t: Walker Evans: The Getty Museum Collection
items.d: Walker Evans is widely recognized as one of the greatest American photographers of the twentieth century, and the J. Paul Getty Museum owns one of the most comprehensive collections of his work, including more of his vintage prints than any other museum in the world. This lavishly illustrated volume brings together for the first time all of the Museum’s Walker Evans holdings. Included here are familiar images—such as

items.t: Introduction to Imaging
items.a: Howard Besser.  Revision Edited by Sally Hubbard with Deborah Lenert
items.d: The first edition of Introduction to Imaging was published in 1995 and quickly became a standard textbook on the construction of digital image collections. The Visual Resources Association Bulletin praised it for setting forth “important basic principles and technical terms that anyone beginning an imaging project would need to know.” Significantly expanded and updated, the revised edition of Introduction to Imaging

items.t: Managing Change: Sustainable Approaches to the Conservation of the Built Environment
items.a: Edited by Jeanne Marie Teutonico and Frank Matero
items.d:
Since the 1970s, sustainability has evolved as a significant mode of thought in nearly every field of intellectual activity. In 1992 the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro brought the ideas of sustainability and development to the forefront of global politics.
For historic resources—whether a cultural landscape, town, building, or work of art—which cannot be physically regener

items.t: Painted Love: Prostitution in French Art of the Impressionist Era
items.d: Prostitution was widespread in nineteenth-century Paris and, as French streets filled with these women of the night, French art and literature of the period took notice. This engrossing book explains why, providing the first description and analysis of French artistic interest in women prostitutes and examining how the subject was treated in the art of the 1870s and 1880s by such avant-garde painters as Cézanne, Dega

items.t: Edgar Degas: Waiting
items.d: Degas's pastel Waiting (L'Attente) is an extraordinary object in its craftsmanship and color, as well as in the emotional pull it immediately exerts upon the viewer. But in addition to those qualities that we expect from a great work of art, Waiting also has an aura of ambiguity and even mystery. Both its aesthetic qualities and the deeper questions the work arouses are the subjects of this study by Richard Thomson.

items.t: Joachim Wtewael: Mars and Venus Surprised by Vulcan
items.d: The Dutch artist Joachim Wtewael was a history painter especially admired for his astonishing small paintings on copper. The Getty Museum's Mars and Venus Surprised by Vulcan is one of his finest works in this unusually demanding medium. Though only eight inches high, this Mannerist painting contains eleven figures in three different spaces, captured in a dramatically complex moment from the famous story told by Ovid

items.t: Statuts et Privilèges du Corps des Marchands Orfèvres-Joyailliers: An 18th-Century Compendium of the Laws Governing Silversmithing in France
items.a: Pierre Le Roy; introduction by Paul Micio
items.d: By the eighteenth century, hundreds of laws governing silversmithing in France had been enacted. Many, however, had become outdated or were no longer enforced. The master smith Pierre Le Roy codified, for the first time ever, all of the applicable regulations into a single volume. Originally compiled in 1734, the book was revised in 1759, and it is this definitive version that is published here in a facsimile edition

items.t: The Spitz Master: A Parisian Book of Hours
items.d: The Spitz Hours is one of the Getty’s finest French books of hours. It is also one of the most original and inventive manuscripts in the International style. In new art historical research Gregory Clark places this book’s vivid, even witty, imagery in the turbulent context of Parisian culture around 1420. items.t: A Guide to the Preventive Conservation of Photograph Collections
items.d: More than thirty years of continuing research into the preservation of photographic collections have led to a better understanding of the fragility of these images and the means by which to preserve them. items.t: Personal Viewpoints: Thoughts about Paintings Conservation
items.d:
Bringing innovative scientific techniques to an aesthetic endeavor, paintings conservators face countless decisions as they implement a course of treatment for each picture in their care. 
The papers in this book, originally presented at a seminar organized by the Getty in 2001, explore the values, assumptions, and goals that shape the work of paintings conservators. Six conservators, three curators, and a conservat

items.t: Illuminating the Renaissance: The Triumph of Flemish Manuscript Painting in Europe
items.a: Edited by Thomas Kren and Scot McKendrick
items.d: This comprehensive and richly illustrated catalogue focuses on the finest illustrated manuscripts produced in Europe during the great epoch in Flemish illumination. During th is aesthetically fertile period—beginning in 1467 with the reign of the Burgundian duke Charles the Bold and ending in 1561 with the death of the artist Simon Bening—the art of book painting was raised to a new level of sophistication. Sharing i

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: The Getty Conservation Institute: The First Ten Years, Part 2
items.a: With contributions from Mahasti Afshar, Neville Agnew, Janet Bridgland, Miguel Angel Corzo, Kathleen Dardes, Marta de la Torre, Martha Demas, James R. Druzik, W
items.d: This is the second part of two special issues of Conservation that mark the tenth anniversary of the Getty Conservation Institute. It contains articles about the GCI’s areas of focus: Objects & Collections; Archaeological Sites & Monuments; Historic Structures & Cities; and Public Awareness & Advocacy. Also featured is a conversation with Miguel Angel Corzom the GCI’s Director.

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: The Getty Conservation Institute: The First Ten Years, Part 1
items.a: With contributions from Janet Bridgland and Harold Williams
items.d: This special issue (the first of two) contains a feature article about the first ten years of the Getty Conservation Institute and a conversation with Harold Williams, the Getty Trust’s President and Chief Executive Officer.

items.d: This issue contains a feature about conservation at the crossroads; a conversation with Lawrence Reger, president of the National Institute for the Conservation of Cultural Property; and articles on disaster response in the United States, and the Conservation Institute’s efforts together with the government of Tanzania to preserve the fossil footprints at Laetoli.

items.d: Although Hermann Murhesius is best known today in Anglo-American architectural literature for his studies of the English house, these were only one aspect of a more encompassing modernist polemic emanating from the German realist movement of the late 1890s. items.t: Julia Margaret Cameron: The Complete Photographs
items.a: Julian Cox and Colin Ford, with contributions by Joanne Lukitsh and Philippa Wright
items.d: According to one of Julia Margaret Cameron’s great-nieces, “we never knew what Aunt Julia was going to do next, nor did anyone else.” This is an accurate summation of the life of the British photographer (1815–1879), who took up the camera at age forty-eight and made more than twelve hundred images during a fourteen-year career. Living at the height of the Victorian era, Cameron was anything but conventional, experim

items.t: Friedrich Gilly: Essays on Architecture, 1796–1799
items.a: Introduction by Fritz Neumeyer, Translation by David Britt
items.d: When Friedrich Gilly died in 1800, at the age of twenty-eight, he had published only four short essays, and his executed works consisted of a few minor buildings still under construction. The influence he exerted on Berlin architects active during the first half of the nineteenth century, however, justifies regarding him as the founder of the Berlin architectural tradition. items.t: Italian and Spanish Sculpture: Catalogue of the J. Paul Getty Museum Collection
items.a: Peggy Fogelman and Peter Fusco with contributions by Marietta Cambareri
items.d: Since the sculpture department was established in 1984, the J. Paul Getty Museum’s holdings have grown to encompass some 170 works ranging in date from the Renaissance through the nineteenth century, with particular strengths in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century bronzes and Neoclassical works in marble and terracotta. items.t: Claiming the Stones/Naming the Bones: Cultural Property and the Negotiation of National and Ethnic Identity
items.a: Edited by Elazar Barkan and Ronald Bush
items.d:
Cultural property such as works of art, monuments, literature, sacred remains, and traditional practices can create a profound sense of communal belonging, yet nothing illuminates the ambiguities of group identity more powerfully than conflicting claims to such material.
This volume addresses current controversies over various kinds of cultural property from the perspectives of archaeology, physical anthropology, et

items.t: James Ensor: Christ's Entry into Brussels in 1889
items.d: The brash young artist James Ensor painted Christ's Entry into Brussels in 1889 during a period of extraordinary artistic and political fomentation in his native Belgium. It is one of the most dazzling, innovative, and perplexing paintings created in Europe in the late nineteenth century, rivaling any work of its period in audacity and ambition. Huge in scale, complex in design and execution, and brimming with social

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: A Masterpiece in Prague
items.a: With contributions from Miguel Angel Corzo; Eliška Fuĉíková, William S. Ginell, Václav Havel, Jeffrey Levin, and Barbara Roberts

items.d: This issue contains a feature about Mexican painter David Alfaro Siqueiros’s 1932 América Tropical mural; a conversation with Henry G. Cisneros, the U.S. Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, on historic preservation; and articles on historic preservation in Los Angeles after the 1994 Northridge earthquake, and “Picture L.A.,” a photography project aimed at a new generation of Angelenos.

items.a: With contributions from Marta de la Torre, Martha Demas, Jeffrey Levin, Dev Mehta, and Jane Slate Siena
items.d: This issue contains a feature that shares research on the preservation of temple grottoes spread throughout Asia and on the site conservation of Mogao; a conversation with Dev Mehta, the commissioner of the Bombay Metropolitan Region Development Authority; and articles about a recent cultural heritage conference in Colombo, Sri Lanka, and a GCI project in collaboration with archaeologists and government authorities i

items.t: Introduction to Art Image Access: Tools, Standards, and Strategies
items.d: With the proliferation of information on the World Wide Web and in other networked environments, one of the main things that users search for are images of works of art and architecture. End-users generally try to search for images by subject, a process that often proves unsatisfactory and frustrating. items.t: The Archaeology of Colonialism
items.a: Edited by Claire L. Lyons and John K. Papadopoulos
items.d:
The Archaeology of Colonialism demonstrates how artifacts are not only the residue of social interaction but also instrumental in shaping identities and communities.

items.d: Pieter Saenredam (1597–1665) was one of the magical painters of 17th-century Holland, a time known as the Golden Age of Dutch Art. items.d: Pigments, corrosion products, and minerals are usually considered separately, either as painting materials or as the deterioration products of metals, even though they are often the same compounds. This 190-year review of the literature on copper and its alloys integrates that information across a broad spectrum of interests that are all too frequently compartmentalized. items.t: European Drawings 4: Catalogue of the Collections
items.d:
The Getty Museum's collection of drawings was begun in 1981 with the purchase of a Rembrandt nude; it has since become one of the world's most important repositories of European works from the fifteenth through the nineteenth century. 
This fourth volume of the catalogue of the drawings collection reproduces and describes all the works acquired by the Getty Museum from 1995 to 1998, a time when particular emphasis w

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: Preserving a Historic City
items.a: With contributions from Mahasti Afshar, Jorge E. Sciupac, Jane Slate Siena, and Jamil Mahuad Witt
items.d: This issue contains a feature about the architecture of Ecuador’s capital city of Quito; a conversation with Jamil Mahuad Witt, mayor of Quito; and articles about a recent international colloquium on earthquakes held in Quito, and a conference in Cairo devoted to funding and technical support for earthquake damage.

items.t: Conservation, The GCI Newsletter: The Preservation of Information
items.a: With contributions from James R. Druzik, Jeffrey Levin, Jane Slate Siena, Elizabeth Gay Teoman, and Peter Waters
items.d: This issue contains a feature about the preservation of information; a conversation with Elizabeth Gay Teoman, director of the Los Angeles Public Library; and articles on “phased conservation” and a recent research initiative for preservation in libraries.

items.t: Empathy, Form, and Space: Problems in German Aesthetics, 1873–1893

items.a: With contributions from Mitchell Bishop, Wolf-Dieter Dube; Eric F. Hansen, Jeffrey Levin, Margaret G. H. MacLean, and Frank Preusser

items.a: Michael K. Rust and Janice M. Kennedy
items.d: Surveys of natural history and art museums indicate that beetles belonging to the families Anobiidae and Dermestidae and moths belonging to the family Tineidae are major pests. items.t: The Terracottas of the Tarantine Greeks
items.d: Working in shops near shrines and temples in the ancient city of Tarentum, the coroplasts, or figurine modelers, produced enormous numbers of figurines for use by worshipers as votive or funeral offerings. Presented here is the small collection of molds and figurines from southern Italy now in the possession of the Getty Museum, with an expert discussion focusing on the original form and function of the figures.

items.t: The Conservation of Ancient Marble
items.d: This is the first publication in a projected series dealing with the care of fine artworks. In it, David Rinne describes common problems encountered when conserving marble objects and the appropriate treatments, beginning with the surface and progressing through to the center. The last section of the text explains elements of treatment, such as disassembly, reconstruction, and the final state of the sculpture.

items.d: The richness of Near Eastern art is epitomized by sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Persian carpets. Among the finest ever produced, the two Ardabil carpets are believed to have been made as offerings for the Shrine of Sheikh Safi at Ardabil during the Safavid dynasty in sixteenth-century Persia. items.t: Giovanni di Francesco and the Master of Pratovecchio
items.d: The Getty Museum’s curator of paintings traces the provenance of the so-called Poggibonsi Altarpiece, one of the Museum's fifteenth-century triptychs, attributing it to Giovanni di Francesco. He also discusses the possible identification of Giovanni as the Master of Pratovecchio and catalogues works attributed to both painters that form part of other museum collections.

items.d: This volume catalogues the major antiquities—sculpture, frescoes, and mosaics—acquired by 1972 by the J. Paul Getty Museum.

items.t: The Cassone Paintings of Francesco di Giorgio
items.d: The wood-paneled chests, or cassoni, painted by Francesco di Giorgio early in his career are thought to represent the pinnacle of his achievements. This monograph treats Francesco’s fifteenth-century cassone paintings in terms of chronology, iconography, and overall importance; included is his Triumph of Chastity, now in the collection of the Getty Museum.

items.t: The Statue of Cybele in the J. Paul Getty Museum
items.d: This book examines a statue of the Roman mother goddess Cybele in the collection of the J. Paul Getty Museum. The author discusses the style and iconography of the statue and proposes ultimately that it is a divine likeness of Livia, wife of the first Roman emperor Augustus.

items.d: This book is intended to introduce and guide visitors to the painting collection of the J. Paul Getty Museum. The collection includes Tuscan (Florentine and Sienese) paintings of the fifteenth century, Venetian works from the sixteenth century, and Dutch and Flemish paintings from the seventeenth century.

In addition to providing an historical background information essential to understanding these beautiful objects, specific examples from the Met's collection are discussed in detail.

items.d: The outcome of experiments in the examination of works of art under ultra-violet rays, conducted in the Museum in the late 1920s by James J. Rorimer

items.t: A Handbook of Mohammedan Decorative Arts
items.d: This publication from 1930 highlights The Metropolitan Museum of Art's strong Islamic art collection with over 170 works discussed.

items.t: Catalogue of European Court Swords and Hunting Swords Including the De Dino, Riggs, and Reubell Collections
items.d: This volume describes and illustrates court swords and hunting swords that form part of the collection of arms exhibited by The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

items.t: Catalogue of European Daggers including the Ellis, De Dino, Riggs and Reubell collections
items.d: This catalogue numerous examples of daggers dating from the 14th to the 18th century and also provides a broader history of daggers in general.

items.t: Handbook of the Pierpont Morgan Wing
items.d: Historic photographs of the galleries provide insight into the history of the Pierpont Morgan Wing, with political, social, and economic contexts.

items.t: The James F. Ballard Collection of Oriental Rugs
items.d: This catalogue illustrates and discusses 125 carpets from Persia, India, Turkey, the Caucasus, Central Asia, and Spain, spanning the 15th to early 19th century.

items.t: Helmets and Body Armor in Modern Warfare
items.d: This book presents the virtues and failings of helmets and body armor in warfare of the time.
